subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: Entering the Poem — Prayer, Wish, and Hope

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.52): distinguish wish, hope, and prayer aloud.
Let us discuss (p.53): silent reading, underline agreed lines, share in groups.

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the three sentences from 'Let us read' aloud (p.52) and asks students which feels most like a prayer and why. Students call out their choices briefly, and the teacher draws out the difference between wishing, hoping, and praying.

Teacher reads the full poem aloud at a measured pace while students follow in their books (p.52–53). Students then read it silently a second time, underlining any line they personally agree with or find moving.

Students share their underlined lines in small groups from 'Let us discuss' (p.53). Each group identifies which line was chosen by the most members and a spokesperson shares it with the class, giving a brief reason.

Teacher closes by asking: what makes this poem feel like a prayer rather than an ordinary poem? Two or three students respond briefly; the teacher notes the key idea — the speaker is asking, not commanding — on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem opens with the speaker's aspiration to treat friendship as the most important thing in her life, a devotional tone reinforced by the AABB rhyme scheme. Students often conflate wish and prayer; the opening task is designed precisely to surface that distinction before the poem is read. Any line may be underlined — the activity values personal response, not a single correct answer.

periods.activity_title: Reading Closely — Stanzas, Summary, and Feeling

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.54): circle correct highlighted words to complete poem summary.
Let us think and reflect (p.54): answer in one word — how the poet feels, what she uses.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.54): write one reason why this poem is a prayer.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the poem aloud once, then asks students to keep their books open at p.54 for the summary-completion task.

Students work individually on 'Let us discuss' (p.54), circling the correct highlighted word from each pair to complete the poem summary. Teacher circulates, pausing to discuss any pair students find genuinely difficult — for example, 'heart' versus 'mind' as the organ the speaker wants to understand friendship.

Class moves to 'Let us think and reflect' (p.54): two one-word answer questions. Teacher takes answers orally first — 'blessed' and 'heart' — and asks students to explain in a sentence why the poem gives those answers before they write them down.

Teacher sets the homework task: write one sentence explaining why this poem is a prayer, drawing on any line from the poem. Students note it in their exercise books and the teacher briefly signals what a good answer might attend to — the form of address and the requesting language.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's central image of the heart as an organ of understanding ('Let me use my heart to see') is the most intellectually rich moment; do not rush past the heart/mind choice in the summary task. The one-word answer items are deliberately simple — they build confidence before the more demanding extract analysis in the next unit.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.54): three questions on stanza 3 — speaker's character, method, feeling.
Let us think and reflect (p.55): three questions on stanzas 4–5 — feelings, thoughtfulness, no judgements.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads stanza 3 ('I want to do much more than share…') aloud twice — once at normal pace, once slowly — and asks students: what does the speaker promise to do?

Students work through the three questions on stanza 3 from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.54): choosing the best character-word, deciding how the speaker will act, and filling in a blank about feeling. Teacher takes answers one at a time, asking students to point to the line that supports each choice.

Teacher reads stanzas 4 and 5 ('Let me use my heart to see… But love my friends the way they are') aloud and pauses to ask: what does 'from afar' mean in the context of making judgements about a friend?

Students answer the three questions on stanzas 4–5 from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.55): identifying the line about using feelings to understand, choosing the character-word, and completing the blank about judgements. Pairs compare answers before a brief whole-class check.
Teacher draws together both extracts: the poem moves from doing ('make their wishes come true') to being ('love my friends the way they are'). Students note this idea briefly in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's most striking idea is unconditional acceptance — 'make no judgements from afar' and 'love my friends the way they are.' Students may need the phrase 'from afar' unpacked: judging a friend from a distance, without truly knowing them, is the opposite of the empathy the poem endorses. Both extract tasks work stanza by stanza, so students who need more time on stanza 3 can be given a minute before the class moves on.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Two Friends — Outdoor Activities

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.56): one-word answer — what the friends purchase at the park bench.
Let us listen (p.56): circle the pictures that match activities described in the passage.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the listening passage: students will hear about outdoor activities two friends, Ajay and Dhiraj, enjoy together. Students open their books to p.56 and look at the six pictures without reading anything yet.

Teacher reads the listening passage aloud at a clear, unhurried pace. Students listen only — no writing. Teacher then reads it a second time; on this reading, students jot down one or two words for the first question from 'Let us listen' (p.56): what do the friends purchase and use on the park bench?
Quick class check on the first question: students give their answer (a comic book); teacher confirms against the passage and asks which word in the passage tells us what they do with it on the bench.

Teacher reads the passage a third time. Students now circle the correct pictures in their textbooks (p.56) for the second task from 'Let us listen' — matching each activity described to the corresponding picture. Pairs compare their circled choices before a whole-class review.

Teacher leads a brief oral wrap: which activity from the passage do students also enjoy with their own friends? Two or three students respond in a sentence each, keeping the conversation natural and unhurried.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript describes six activities: swings/park, slides, nature walks, cycling, eating ice-cream, and reading a comic book on a bench. Students sometimes miss the distinction between individual preferences (Ajay likes slides most; Dhiraj likes nature) and shared activities — worth flagging when checking picture answers. The passage is short enough to be read three times within the available time.

periods.activity_title: Speaking as Friends — Paired Role-Play Conversations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.56–57): paired role-play — park walk and tiffin-sharing conversations.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the speaking task from 'Let us speak' (p.56–57): two paired role-play situations — a walk in the park and sharing tiffins at school. Teacher models the opening of Situation 1 with one student: a greeting, an invitation, and a brief plan. The class notes the key moves: greet, invite, plan, respond.

Pairs enact Situation 1 — the park walk conversation. They greet each other, discuss whether to go, plan activities if yes, or suggest alternatives if no. Teacher circulates and gently prompts pairs who are stuck, using cue phrases from the board.

Pairs switch to Situation 2 — the tiffin-sharing conversation. They describe their tiffin contents, express a wish to share, say how sharing makes them feel, appreciate their friend's food, and close with thanks. Teacher notes any student who uses a particularly natural or expressive phrase for the wrap-up.

Two or three pairs perform one of their conversations briefly for the class. Teacher gives short, encouraging feedback — noting one thing done well and one language point to refine — without singling out errors.

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking tasks are framed around real friendship situations, which connects naturally to the poem's emphasis on sharing and caring. Students who hesitate should be paired with a confident partner and given the first line of their greeting as a prompt; the constitution of this class allows every student space to express themselves without pressure. Task 2 from 'Let us speak' — creating an entirely new situation — is left unanchored here; students who finish early may attempt it independently.
materials: Board with key conversational cue phrases

periods.activity_title: Writing a Paragraph — How Our Friendship Began

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.57): list answers to When/Where/How, then write an 80-word paragraph with a title.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the writing task from 'Let us write' (p.57) aloud and explains the three-step structure: answer When, Where, and How first as brief notes, then build sentences, then shape a paragraph. Teacher does a quick shared example on the board, sketching answers to the three questions about an imaginary friendship.

Students work individually on the planning step: writing short answers to When, Where, and How their own friendship started. Teacher circulates to help students who are unsure what counts as a 'how' — the circumstances, the first conversation, a shared activity.

Students draft their paragraph of approximately 80 words using their planning notes. They also choose a title. Teacher circulates, encouraging students to connect their notes into flowing sentences rather than a list, and to use at least one specific detail — a place name, a subject, a shared memory.
Students exchange books with a partner for a paired read. The partner marks one detail they found interesting and checks that the paragraph has a clear title. Students make any quick improvements.
Two or three volunteers read their titles and opening sentence aloud. Teacher affirms the variety of beginnings and collects books for a written response if time permits.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task asks students to narrate a personal experience, which aligns with the poem's theme of valuing specific, real friendships rather than an abstract ideal. Some students may not recall a single founding moment; they should be encouraged to describe the circumstances under which they first became close. All drafting, peer response and revision happen within this sitting — no continuation is assumed.

periods.activity_title: Words for Friendship — Synonyms and Qualities

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.55): select words similar in meaning to 'blessed' from the given list.
Let us learn (p.55–56): complete partial words for friend qualities, then fill in five sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'blessed' on the board and reads the line from the poem ('With special friends I feel I'm blessed') aloud. Students suggest what the word means in their own words before the task begins.

Students work on the first task from 'Let us learn' (p.55): selecting from the list — excited, grateful, understood, thankful, relaxed — which words are similar in meaning to 'blessed.' The class discusses each choice: why 'grateful' and 'thankful' qualify, and why 'excited' and 'relaxed' do not, grounding the discussion in how the word is used in the poem.

Students turn to the second task from 'Let us learn' (p.55–56): completing the partially spelled words for five friend qualities (loyal, helpful, kind, caring, honest) and then filling those words into five sentences. Teacher reads each sentence aloud before students write, so the context is clear.

Quick oral check: teacher reads each sentence stem and calls on a student for the answer. Class confirms together. Teacher closes by asking which of the five qualities appears in the poem, even if not by name — drawing a brief connection back to the poem's language.

periods.teacher_notes: The vocabulary task grounds 'blessed' in the poem's second stanza before moving to a broader list of friendship qualities; this sequencing helps students see vocabulary as emerging from a text, not as an isolated list. Task 3 from 'Let us learn' — writing three sentences about three friends — is not anchored here; students who finish early may attempt it independently as a stretch activity.

periods.activity_title: Friendship Quotations — Meaning, Memory, and Display

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.58): discuss meaning of two friendship quotations; share a personal experience.
Let us explore (p.58): find, write, colour and decorate a friendship quotation for the class board.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes both quotations on the board: 'A friend in need is a friend indeed' and 'My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me.' Students read them silently, then the class discusses meaning — what each quotation is claiming about friendship and whether the two ideas are similar or different.

Students work in pairs to recall a personal experience that fits either quotation from 'Let us explore' (p.58). Pairs share briefly with another pair, then two or three pairs share with the whole class. Teacher draws a short comparison: how do these real experiences echo what the poem says about caring and accepting friends?

Students search their memory or the classroom's available resources (dictionaries, the textbook's reference pages) for one friendship quotation — it may be in their own language. They write it on a piece of paper, then colour and decorate it to display on the class board. Teacher circulates and helps students who cannot recall a quotation by offering two or three from the board as starting points.

Students hold up their decorated quotations briefly; three or four are pinned to the class board as a display. Teacher closes by connecting the range of quotations back to the poem's core idea — that friendship calls for active, selfless effort.

periods.teacher_notes: The two textbook quotations offer contrasting emphases: one defines friendship through action in difficulty, the other through mutual growth. Students who find it hard to recall a personal experience matching either quotation should not be pressed — the act of choosing which quotation resonates more is itself a valid response. All making and displaying happens within this sitting; no prior material is assumed.

periods.activity_title: Closing the Poem — Reflection, Discussion, and Personal Prayer

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.54–55): why does the speaker want to do more for her friend?
Let us think and reflect (p.55): do you also pray for your friend — what do you wish?
Let us speak (p.56–57): a brief guided conversation sharing what students would wish for a friend.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem aloud once more, from beginning to end, at the same measured pace as the opening reading. Students follow silently, and the teacher invites them to notice any line that means more to them now than it did on first reading.

Class discussion on the question from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.54–55): why does the speaker want to do more than simply share her friends' hopes and plans? Teacher guides students to see the difference between passive companionship and active support, drawing on stanza 3. Students give answers in two or three sentences.

Students respond to the discussion question from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.55): do they also pray for their friends, and what would they wish? Students think for a moment, then share in pairs before two or three speak to the whole class. Teacher acknowledges the range of wishes without evaluating content.

Guided conversation from 'Let us speak' (p.56–57): in pairs, students take turns telling their partner one specific wish they would make for them — using the sentence frame 'I wish for you…' or 'May you always…'. Teacher circulates and notes the variety of register students use, gently drawing attention to the prayer-like phrasing where it appears.

Teacher closes by asking: what is the most important single idea in the poem? Students give one-word or one-phrase answers — acceptance, empathy, care, effort. Teacher writes the words on the board as a collective summary of the poem's meaning.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the poem's stanzas in detail in earlier units, students are now ready to discuss the poem's larger argument: that friendship is an active, self-giving commitment rather than a passive feeling. The question about whether the speaker knows her friends' wishes (task index 9 in the summary) is left unanchored here and may be treated as a self-study prompt — students who wish to explore it independently are directed to p.55 of their textbook.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets layers of meaning in a lyric poem using close reading and discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jill Wolf's prayer-poem on selfless friendship, unconditional acceptance, empathy, AABB rhyme.
items.item_stem: In the poem, the speaker uses a specific organ — not the mind — to understand what friends can truly be. Which line from the poem most clearly expresses this idea?

options.label: A
options.text: May my friendships always be / The most important thing to me.

options.label: B
options.text: Let me use my heart to see, / To realise what friends can be.

options.label: C
options.text: I'll try all that a friend can do / To make their wishes come true.

options.label: D
options.text: With special friends I feel I'm blessed.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may be focusing on the poem's opening declaration rather than the specific image of empathy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student identifies the poem's theme of effort, but confuses active doing with the separate idea of feeling and understanding.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student picks up the idea of being blessed by friendship, but misses the specific empathy image the question targets.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and interprets layers of meaning in a lyric poem using close reading and discussion as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jill Wolf's prayer-poem on selfless friendship, unconditional acceptance, empathy, AABB rhyme.
items.item_stem: The poem ends with the lines on page 53 beginning "And make no judgements from afar." What do you think the speaker means by judging a friend "from afar"? Why does the speaker consider this wrong? Support your answer with evidence from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Judging a friend 'from afar' means forming opinions about them without truly knowing them or making an effort to understand their feelings. The speaker considers this wrong because the whole poem argues for active empathy and unconditional acceptance — 'love my friends the way they are' — which is the opposite of distant, uninformed judgement.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short spoken passage and retrieves specific information to respond accurately using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Ajay and Dhiraj's shared outdoor activities: cycling, nature walks, ice-cream, comic-book reading.
items.item_stem: Listen to the talk about Ajay and Dhiraj. Which of the following statements about their activities is true?

options.text: Ajay enjoys the slides in the park the most.
Both friends go cycling on Sundays.
Dhiraj enjoys listening to birds during their walks.
The friends read a storybook together on the park bench.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — the passage states Ajay enjoys slides the most.
2. False — the passage says they go cycling on Saturdays, not Sundays.
3. True — the passage says Dhiraj likes nature, so both listen to birds during their walks.
4. False — the passage says they purchase a comic book, not a storybook.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short spoken passage and retrieves specific information to respond accurately using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Ajay and Dhiraj's shared outdoor activities: cycling, nature walks, ice-cream, comic-book reading.
items.item_stem: Based on the listening passage about Ajay and Dhiraj, what do both friends truly enjoy the most, and what does this tell you about their friendship? Answer in two to three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: What both friends truly enjoy the most is eating ice-cream together. This suggests their friendship is built on simple shared pleasures rather than grand activities. The passage also shows they share each other's interests — for example, both take nature walks because Dhiraj likes nature — which reflects mutual care.

items.item_stem: With a partner, act out the following situation: You meet your friend at school and want to share your tiffin with them. Greet your friend, describe what you have brought, invite them to share, and tell them how sharing makes you feel. Speak for at least five turns each.

expected_elements: Uses an appropriate greeting to open the conversation.
Names at least one specific food item from their tiffin.
Expresses a wish to share using polite or friendly language.
States how sharing makes them feel, using a full sentence.

items.item_stem: The poem says the speaker wants to 'love her friends the way they are.' Imagine a friend has a habit you find a little annoying — for example, always being late or talking too much. Role-play a conversation in which you kindly accept your friend as they are, without making them feel judged. One of you plays the friend, the other the speaker from the poem. Be ready to explain to the class why you chose the words you did.

expected_elements: Acknowledges the friend's habit without criticism or judgement.
Uses warm, accepting language that reflects the poem's tone.
Gives at least one reason for valuing the friend despite the habit.
Can explain their word choices when asked by the teacher.

items.source_context: Personal paragraph (~80 words) describing how a friendship started — When, Where, How.
items.item_stem: The poet writes, "I want to do much more than share / The hopes and plans of friends who care." Think of a time when you did something kind or helpful for a friend — not just sharing, but going out of your way for them. Write a paragraph of about 80 words describing what you did, why you did it, and how it made both of you feel. Give your paragraph a title.

expected_elements: Describes a specific act of kindness, not a general statement.
Explains the reason for the act, showing awareness of a friend's need.
Includes how the writer and the friend both felt after the act.
Paragraph has a title and is approximately 80 words.

items.source_context: Synonyms for 'blessed'; friendship-quality vocabulary: loyal, helpful, kind, caring, honest.
items.item_stem: Match each friendship quality in Column A with the sentence in Column B that best shows that quality.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|----------|----------|
| loyal | She always tells the truth, even when it is difficult. |
| caring | He has supported his friend for many years without changing. |
| honest | She noticed her friend was sad and stayed to listen. |
| kind | He shared his lunch with a classmate who had nothing to eat. |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: loyal – He has supported his friend for many years without changing, honest – She always tells the truth even when it is difficult, caring – She noticed her friend was sad and stayed to listen, kind – He shared his lunch with a classmate who had nothing to eat.

answer_key.right: He has supported his friend for many years without changing.
She noticed her friend was sad and stayed to listen.
She always tells the truth, even when it is difficult.
He shared his lunch with a classmate who had nothing to eat.

items.source_lo: Student identifies synonyms and context-appropriate vocabulary drawn from the poem's language as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Synonyms for 'blessed'; friendship-quality vocabulary: loyal, helpful, kind, caring, honest.
items.item_stem: The poem says "With special friends I feel I'm blessed." The word 'blessed' can be replaced by words that carry a similar meaning. Read the two sentences below. In each sentence, choose the word from the brackets that best replaces 'blessed' and explain in one sentence why that word fits better than the other. (a) "With special friends I feel I'm [grateful / excited]." (b) "With special friends I feel I'm [thankful / relaxed]."

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (a) 'Grateful' fits better than 'excited' because 'blessed' in the poem carries a sense of deep appreciation for something precious, not the short-lived energy of excitement. (b) 'Thankful' fits better than 'relaxed' because the speaker is expressing heartfelt recognition of her friends' value, which is closer to thankfulness than to a state of calm.

items.source_context: Two friendship quotations; finding, decorating, and displaying a chosen friendship quotation.
items.item_stem: Read the two friendship quotations below and answer the questions that follow. (i) "A friend in need is a friend indeed." (ii) "My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me." (a) What does each quotation say about what a true friend does? Write one sentence for each. (b) Which quotation connects more closely to the ideas in the poem "A Friend's Prayer"? Give one reason from the poem to support your answer.

expected_elements: Explains the meaning of both quotations in own words, one sentence each.
Identifies one quotation as closer to the poem and names it explicitly.
Cites a specific line or idea from the poem as supporting evidence.
Writing is in complete sentences and uses appropriate vocabulary.

items.source_lo: Student interprets and applies friendship quotations to personal experience using hands-on extension as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Two friendship quotations; finding, decorating, and displaying a chosen friendship quotation.
items.item_stem: Find one famous quotation about friendship — it may be in English or in your own language. Write it down neatly on a piece of paper. Below the quotation, write three to four sentences explaining: (a) what the quotation means, (b) how it connects to something you have experienced with a friend, and (c) why you chose this particular quotation. Colour and decorate the paper so it can be displayed on the class board.

expected_elements: Quotation is written clearly and credited to a source or speaker if known.
Explanation covers all three points: meaning, personal connection, reason for choice.
Personal experience is specific, not a general statement about friendship.
Decoration is neat and the writing is legible for display.
